```{=html}
<p>Energy made: the 24 outputs add up to 676 MWh. Capacity factor: 676 ÷ (100 × 24) = 28.2%. The night hours count too.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The power curve of an illustrative 3 MW wind turbine</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Below 3 m/s</b> (cut-in): no electricity.</li>
<li><b>3 to 12 m/s</b> (rated): output follows the cube of the wind speed; doubling a speed within this range gives eight times the output.</li>
<li><b>12 to 25 m/s</b> (cut-out): output holds at 3,000 kW.</li>
<li><b>Above 25 m/s</b>: the turbine shuts down to protect itself.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you work through this step by step: a year of output, the solar day, the turbine's power curve and a quick calculation.</p>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="t5-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Capacity factor</dt><dd>Energy made ÷ (size × hours): the share of the most a plant could make that it actually made.</dd>
<dt>Same MW, different MWh</dt><dd>In 2025, U.S. nuclear plants ran at 91.1% of their size on average, wind at 33.8% and solar at 24.0%.</dd>
<dt>Every hour counts</dt><dd>Nights and calm hours stay in the count, which is why solar's capacity factor is low.</dd>
<dt>The cube law</dt><dd>Between cut-in (3 m/s) and rated speed (12 m/s), twice the wind speed gives this turbine eight times the output.</dd>
<dt>Rated and cut-out speeds</dt><dd>From the rated speed to cut-out (25 m/s) the output holds at 3,000 kW; above cut-out the turbine shuts down.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Capacity factor depends on the period and the place</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Every fleet's capacity factor changes from month to month. U.S. averages in 2025 (EIA, Table 6.07.B):

| Fleet | Lowest month | Highest month |
|---|---|---|
| Wind | 23.1% (September) | 43.1% (March) |
| Solar | 13.1% (December) | 31.9% (June and July) |
| Nuclear | 81.0% (October) | 99.2% (December) |

Nuclear dips in spring and fall, the seasons when many reactors stop to refuel.

- **Availability is not capacity factor.** A solar farm can be ready all night and still make nothing.
- **Curtailment lowers it.** A wind farm turned down by the grid makes less than its weather allowed ([lesson 0](00-grid-operator.qmd)).
- **Sites differ.** The U.S. averages hide windy plains and sunny deserts; Prairie Town's shapes come from one region.

[Lesson 7](07-cost.qmd) uses capacity factor to spread a plant's building cost over the MWh it makes.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The power curve, from physics to measurements</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

**Power in the wind.** Through a rotor, the wind carries $P_\text{wind} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$. With the units below this gives watts; divide by 1,000 for kilowatts.

| Symbol | Meaning | The lesson's turbine |
|---|---|---|
| $\rho$ | air density, kg/m³ | 1.225 kg/m³, sea level |
| $A$ | area the blades sweep, m² | 7,854 m², a 100 m rotor |
| $v$ | wind speed, m/s | 12 m/s, its rated speed |
| $P_\text{wind}$ | power in the wind, W | about 8,313,000 W, or 8,313 kW |

**What the turbine captures.** It makes 3,000 kW at 12 m/s, so its [power coefficient]{.lx-term term="power-coefficient"} is $C_p = 3{,}000 / 8{,}313 = 0.36$.

**The Betz limit.** No rotor can capture more than $16/27 \approx 0.593$ of the wind's power.

**The lesson's clean [power curve]{.lx-term term="power-curve"}**, output $P$ in kW at wind speed $v$ in m/s:

$$
P(v) = \begin{cases}
3000 \times (v/12)^3 \text{ kW} & 3 \le v < 12 \text{ m/s}\\
3000 \text{ kW} & 12 \le v \le 25 \text{ m/s}\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$

**A measured curve.** Real 10-minute averages scatter around a curve: gusts, air density and the turbine's own controls move each one.

Each point below averages the records with similar wind speeds (a 0.5 m/s bin). The spread is one [standard deviation]{.lx-term term="standard-deviation"} of those records: how much they vary, not an error bar on the average.

The chart shows a 1.5 MW research turbine that NREL tested in 2011, beside a clean curve built the same way for it: the cube law at its best $C_p$, 0.52, capped at 1,500 kW.

```{=html}
<div id="t5-measured" class="lx5-measured">
<table class="lx-mini-table">
<caption>Measured against clean, selected wind speeds (the full table appears with JavaScript on)</caption>
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Wind speed, m/s</th><th scope="col">Measured average, kW</th><th scope="col">Spread (±1 standard deviation), kW</th><th scope="col">Clean curve, kW</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>3.97</td><td>59</td><td>28</td><td>93</td></tr>
<tr><td>5.99</td><td>304</td><td>52</td><td>319</td></tr>
<tr><td>8.00</td><td>742</td><td>74</td><td>759</td></tr>
<tr><td>10.03</td><td>1,200</td><td>75</td><td>1,497</td></tr>
<tr><td>11.98</td><td>1,400</td><td>127</td><td>1,500</td></tr>
<tr><td>13.97</td><td>1,482</td><td>47</td><td>1,500</td></tr>
<tr><td>15.98</td><td>1,497</td><td>17</td><td>1,500</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
```

From about 6 to 8 m/s the averages follow the cube law closely. Above that they bend over gradually: full power comes near 14 m/s, not at a sharp corner near 10 m/s.

Source: NREL, [Power Performance Test Report for the U.S. Department of Energy 1.5-Megawatt Wind Turbine](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy15osti/63684.pdf), Table 6 (2015; test from February to June 2011).

- **Research.** Estimating a wind farm's curve, with honest error bars, from few records is an active research topic ([Li et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1115/DETC2023-114762); open code: [mfgpr-wind-power-curve](https://github.com/Henryutd2021/mfgpr-wind-power-curve)).
- **Next.** Modeler lesson [M9](m09-surrogates-uq.qmd) fits a curve to data; [bridge B2](b02-python-data.qmd) computes capacity factors in Python.

```{=html}

</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The wind and solar shapes are whole regional fleets, smoother than any single farm.</li>
<li>Wind and solar are reshaped so that each month matches the U.S. average and the best hours reach full size.</li>
<li>The seasons are national; the hours are those of one region.</li>
<li>The nuclear plant's outage and the turbine are illustrative, not a real plant or model.</li>
<li>Air density changes with temperature and altitude, which shifts a real power curve.</li>
<li>The clean curve has no spread: a real turbine's output scatters around it (the measured curve above).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="t5-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="full" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A 100 MW wind farm makes 100 MW most of the time.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In 2025, U.S. wind farms made 33.8% of what they would have made at full size; below rated speed, their output rises and falls roughly with the cube of the wind speed.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="broken" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A solar farm with a 24.0% capacity factor is broken three-quarters of the time.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At night and under clouds it works as designed: the sun, not the machine, sets most of the gap.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="double" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Doubling the wind speed doubles a turbine's output.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. On this lesson's turbine it depends on the speeds:</p>
<ul><li>Both from 3 to 12 m/s: eight times the output (2 × 2 × 2).</li><li>From 12 to 25 m/s: output holds at rated power.</li><li>Above 25 m/s: the turbine shuts down.</li></ul></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="t5">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 50 MW solar farm made 105,120 MWh in a year of 8,760 hours. What was its <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span>?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">24.0%</li><li data-value="b">48.0%</li><li data-value="c">12.0%</li><li data-value="d">100%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>24.0%: 105,120 ÷ (50 × 8,760) = 0.240. Leaving out the night hours would wrongly raise it: capacity factor counts every hour. Using 100 MW would halve it.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mwh" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">At the 2025 U.S. average of 91.1%, how much <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> does 1 MW of nuclear make in a year?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">8,760 MWh</li><li data-value="b">7,980 MWh</li><li data-value="c">911 MWh</li><li data-value="d">91.1 MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>7,980 MWh: 1 MW × 8,760 h × 0.911. The full 8,760 MWh would need every hour at full size.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>EIA publishes these capacity factors every month for every kind of plant. Turning a wind farm's scattered measurements into a power curve with honest error bars is still a research question (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/DETC2023-114762">Li et al., 2023</a>).</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Case file <a href="cf8-power-curves-from-scarce-data.html">CF8</a>: learning a wind turbine's power curve from scarce data.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
```
